A1.justification: Both PDFs describe adversarial inception and Q-Incept, with matching core algorithms, theorems and experiments. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack experiments on four environments, numerical comparisons in Tables 5 and 9, and inception and oracle ablations.

after.justification: v3 reports original experiments on seven environments, state-sanitization defense tests, DQN results, poisoning-rate analyses and computational measurements.

M1.justification: The core Q-Incept procedure remains intact. Appendix A.4.1 adds a DQN adaptation that poisons samples after replay-buffer sampling instead of poisoning trajectories before storage. Section 6.2 also introduces an adaptive attack that trains on SVD-sanitized triggers.

E1.justification: v3 retains the original four environments and adds evaluated Atari Frogger, Pacman and Breakout tasks. Section 6.2 additionally evaluates Q*Bert under state sanitization, introducing a defended observation scenario. DQN evaluation changes the learner configuration rather than adding another task.

E2.justification: v3 adds an evaluated defense, Bharti et al.'s SVD state sanitization, against Q-Incept in Figure 6. TrojDRL, SleeperNets, Q-Vanilla and Oracle-Incept comparisons are retained. BIRD is discussed but not empirically evaluated, and BadRL remains excluded.

E3.justification: The main stealth metric changes from Benign Return Ratio to absolute Benign Return with clean-agent reference scores. Q*Bert's reported main-comparison budgets change from 0.01%/0.03% to 0.1%/0.3%, and Safety Car's trigger changes from a lidar pattern to an appended boolean indicator. DQN victim experiments and SVD-threshold sweeps introduce additional protocols.

E4.justification: v3 adds adaptive-versus-naive trigger tests against sanitization, broader poisoning-rate sensitivity analyses for Q*Bert and CAGE-2, and computational-overhead measurements. The reward-clipping demonstration changes from Highway Merge to Q*Bert and includes Q-Incept. The existing no-inception and oracle ablations remain; the oracle analysis moves to Appendix A.4.3.

E5.justification: Both versions report attack results averaged over five training seeds or runs, with standard deviations. The added DQN results also use five runs. No new confidence-interval, significance-testing or uncertainty-estimation procedure is documented.

E6.justification: v3 adds results for three Atari tasks, defense evasion, throughput and DQN attacks; Table 7 reports DQN ASRs of 92.6% and 88.5% at 0.5% and 1% poisoning. Q*Bert's reported ASR at 0.01% changes from 100% in v1 Table 9 to 21.1% in v3 Table 8, although revised budget reporting prevents establishing a matched-setting regression. v3 also contains conflicting CAGE-2 entries: Tables 3 and 9 report 30.61% versus 30.06% ASR and -44.19 versus -48.64 BR at 0.5% poisoning.

T1.justification: v3 adds explicit benign-transition and reward constraints in Equations 1–2 and inserts a discount factor into the reward-compensation term in Section 4.2, absent from v1 Equation 14. The principal theorems, disjoint-state and bijective-trigger assumptions, and Appendix A.1 proofs otherwise remain essentially unchanged.

C1.justification: The bounded-reward attack-success and stealth claims are retained, but v3 adds the substantial conclusion that no existing defenses are immediately applicable, specifically naming BIRD and state sanitization. v1 calls for future defenses without claiming that existing universal defenses have been defeated. This broadens the paper's central conclusions beyond attack efficacy.

C2.justification: v3 develops explanations linking attack difficulty to action consequences, reward constraints and environment dynamics. It argues that trigger dependence enables evasion of universal defenses, explains why stored poisoned samples become stale under DQN, and acknowledges computational overhead as a possible detection channel. These extend substantially beyond v1's inception and Q-function-accuracy interpretations.

D1.justification: v3 adds a project-code hyperlink, specifies evaluation over 100 trajectories, documents the softmax policy approximation, and provides parameters for the added environments. It also identifies the overhead-test hardware—two RTX 4090 GPUs and a Threadripper 7980x—and measured throughput. These disclosures supplement the core PPO/DQN hyperparameters already present in v1; the code link's accessibility was not externally checked.

R1.justification: Section 2 expands from backdoor attacks and detection into a broader distinction between training-time poisoning and test-time observation, environment and action attacks. Added references include Lu, Rangi, Gleave, Tessler and McMahan. BIRD is newly cited, and state sanitization shifts from background defense literature to a directly challenged approach.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, reward-constraint motivation and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Terminology shifts toward constrained and dynamic rewards; appendix discussion and results are reordered, and the oracle ablation moves out of the main text. The title changes, and acknowledgements and an impact statement are added.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main layout, revises Figure 1, and redesigns the training plots. Table 3 consolidates the previously separated poisoning-budget comparisons into a seven-environment display with raw returns and clean controls. The guarantees table and oracle figure move to the appendix, while new defense figures, result tables and expanded action-manipulation plots are added.

improvement.justification: v3 improves practical validation by testing previously unexamined off-policy adaptation and adaptive defense evasion, exposing poisoning-rate limitations, and measuring computational overhead. Absolute returns, clean controls and additional implementation disclosures improve interpretability and reproducibility. However, conflicting CAGE-2 entries in Tables 3 and 9 weaken numerical confidence, and the conclusion extends to BIRD without a reported BIRD evaluation. These issues temper the overall gains.
